query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy, rapid solidification establishes a finely mixed metastable state in which Mg is initially dissolved within a predominantly solid solution matrix. Under high-temperature or corrosive exposure, the metastable structure undergoes a transformation in which Mg segregates to form discrete intermetallic precipitates (particularly along grain boundaries). These Mg-rich precipitates become preferential sites for oxidation and corrosion, thereby altering the overall corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior of the alloy relative to its as-cast, homogeneous state.
generation.material_initial_state: Rapidly solidified Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy (density < 6 g/cm3) presenting a metastable homogeneous solid solution with incipient/intermixed intermetallic features.
generation.intervention: Controlled thermal exposure (or exposure to high-temperature oxidizing/corrosive environments) that is expected to drive phase evolution.
generation.conditions: Test comparisons are conducted under high-temperature oxidation conditions and in corrosive media (e.g., chloride-containing solutions) while keeping processing histories and bulk density (<6 g/cm3) constant.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation and growth of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates preferentially at grain boundaries and phase interfaces.
generation.mechanism: Thermal activation promotes diffusion-driven segregation of Mg from the supersaturated solid solution; once Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates form, they locally alter the chemical and electrochemical environment, facilitating less protective and more heterogeneous oxide film formation and localized corrosion attack.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the initial as-cast, homogeneous state, the thermally treated alloy will exhibit increased and spatially localized corrosion rates and altered oxidation kinetics (e.g., formation of non-uniform oxides) attributable to the segregation of Mg into intermetallic regions.
generation.baseline: As-cast, non-equilibrium alloy exhibiting a homogeneous, metastable solid solution with minimal Mg segregation and uniform corrosion/oxidation behavior.
generation.boundary: This evolution is expected only under service conditions that provide sufficient thermal or chemical driving force for Mg diffusion; under low-temperature or inert conditions, the transformation and the associated changes in corrosion/oxidation behavior may not occur.
generation.uncertainty: The kinetics and extent of Mg segregation, as well as the precise impact on the micro-scale corrosion and oxidation mechanisms, remain to be quantified. Additionally, the role of accompanying alloying elements in either facilitating or mitigating this transformation is not fully resolved.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of the same Mg-containing lightweight HEA: one in the as-cast (non-equilibrium homogeneous) state and the other subjected to controlled thermal exposure under high-temperature oxidation/corrosive conditions. Use identical sample geometries and processing routes prior to intervention. Assess and compare their microstructures using transmission electron microscopy and energy dispersive spectroscopy to detect Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates. Simultaneously, evaluate corrosion rates (using potentiodynamic polarization) and high-temperature oxidation behavior (via thermogravimetric analysis).
measurements: Grain boundary and phase interface microstructure characterization (TEM/EDX)
Oxidation kinetics and oxide scale morphology via TGA and SEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if no significant increase in Mg segregation (or formation of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates) is observed in the thermally exposed samples compared to the as-cast state, or if the corrosion and oxidation measurements do not show degraded performance (e.g., no statistically significant increase in localized corrosion rates or non-uniform oxide scale formation) in the aged samples under the tested conditions.

Evaluation of Equiatomic CrMnFeCoNiCu System and Subsequent Derivation of a Non-Equiatomic MnFeCoNiCu Alloy

Abstract: AbstractInvestigation into non-equiatomic high-entropy alloys has grown in recent years due to questions about the role of entropy stabilization in forming single-phase solid solutions. Non-equiatomic alloys have been shown to retain the outstanding mechanical properties exhibited by their equiatomic counterparts and even improve electrical, thermal, and magnetic properties, albeit with relaxed composition bounds. However, much remains to understand the processing–structure–property relationships in all classes of so-called high-entropy alloys (HEAs). Here, we are motivated by the natural phenomena of crystal growth and equilibrium conditions to introduce a method of HEA development where controlled processing conditions determine the most probable and stable composition. This is demonstrated by cooling an equiatomic CrMnFeCoNiCu alloy from the melt steadily over 3 days (cooling rate ~4 °C/h). Remarkable Enhanced Mechanical Properties of TiAlCrNbV Medium-Entropy Alloy with Zr Additions

Abstract: Most medium entropy alloys (MEAs) exhibit excellent mechanical properties, but their applications are limited because of their high density. This study explores a series of lightweight nonequiatomic Ti65(AlCrNbV)35-xZrx (x = 3, 5, 7, and 10) MEAs with a low density, high strength, and high ductility. To achieve solid solution strengthening, Zr with a large atomic radius was used. In addition, various thermomechanical treatment parameters were adopted to further improve the MEAs’ mechanical properties. The density of the MEAs was revealed to be approximately 5 g/cm3, indicating that they were lightweight. Through an X-ray diffraction analysis, the MEAs were revealed to have a single body-centered cubic structure not only in the as-cast state but also after thermomechanical treatment. In terms of mechanical properties, all the as-cast MEAs with Zr additions achieved excellent performance (>1000 MPa tensile yield strength and 20% tensile ductility).
